message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The paper is clear and well organised, and Table 1 is internally consistent: the margins match the prices and costs, and the plate counts sum to the stated 1,050. But two of the paper's main arguments rest on errors, and the headline benefit is overstated. I'd fix these before it goes to the owners.

## Major issues

**1. The 12% beef rise is left out of the projection (§4 vs §5.3).**
The paper reports the supplier increase and then ignores it. Taking effect on the same day as the new prices:

| Dish | Cost now | Cost from 1 Apr | Extra cost/week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 | £4.70 | 260 × £0.50 ≈ £131 |
| Steak | £10.40 | £11.65 | 120 × £1.25 ≈ £150 |
| **Total** | | | **≈ £281/week** |

- The net gain is about **£529 a week (~£27,500 a year)**, not £810 (£42,120). That's roughly a third less.
- The steak's margin *falls*, from 60% to about 58% (£28.00 against £11.65). The steak price rise doesn't keep up with its beef cost.
- The ~71% main-course margin only holds if beef costs stay flat. Including the beef rise, main-course margin comes out at roughly **69–70%**. That is barely above today's figure (about 69–70% on my estimate), not a clear step towards the target.

**2. The case for removing the risotto is factually wrong (§5.2).**
The paper says risotto "has the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows it has the **highest** (80%). Its cash profit per plate is £11.20, which beats the burger (£10.80) and the curry (£10.90). It is joint-lowest on sales (90 plates, tied with specials), not uniquely lowest.

There's also a risk the paper doesn't mention. If the risotto is the only regular vegetarian main, removing it could lose whole tables, not just 90 plates. The replacement "seasonal vegetarian special" has no stated cost or margin, so we can't judge whether it's an improvement. The proposal needs a different rationale, or should be dropped.

**3. Trading days are inconsistent (§2 vs §8).**
§2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. §8 says "six trading days a week." One of these is wrong. It doesn't affect the annual figures, since those use 52 weeks, but owners will notice.

## Weaker points

**4. The claim that volumes will hold is asserted, not shown (§5.3, §7).**
- The evidence is one past price change with "no visible effect." The paper doesn't say what it was or how this was measured.
- A useful addition is break-even volumes. For example, fish and chips profit per plate rises from £11.40 to £12.40, so sales could fall about 8% before the increase loses money. The equivalent figures for burger and steak should use post-beef-rise costs.

**5. Some trading claims aren't backed by data.**
"Just under half" of sales on Friday/Saturday dinner and weekday lunch being "a small share" are stated without figures. Both are central to the risk argument in §7. A day-part breakdown would support them.

**6. The link between main-course and overall margin is vague (§1, §5.3).**
The 67% to 70% target is for all food courses, but the paper only addresses mains. It should say whether a 70–71% margin on mains is enough to restore the overall figure, given margins on starters and desserts.

**7. "Not drawing attention" to the increases (§6).**
With 60% repeat custom, regulars will notice anyway. The owners may want to decide this tone explicitly, rather than have it presented as routine.

**8. Fish cost volatility (§4)** is the biggest cost exposure, since fish and chips is the top seller. It deserves a line in §7.

## Smaller points
- The competitor claims check out. All three new prices sit below the midpoint of each range (£17.98, £16.50, £29.50).
- The curry, the third-highest seller, isn't benchmarked against competitors. That's worth noting if it's also underpriced.

## Suggested fixes
1. Restate §5.3 net of the beef increase (~£27,500 a year), and consider pricing the steak at around £29.00 to £29.50 to protect its margin. That is still at or below the competitor midpoint.
2. Rewrite or withdraw §5.2. Risotto is the highest-margin dish.
3. Correct "six trading days" to five.
4. Add break-even volume figures and day-part sales data to support §7.

*Timing note:* the paper is dated March 2026 for a 1 April change. If the changes went ahead, the eight-week monitoring data in §6 should now exist. Comparing actual results against these projections would be more useful to the owners than the forecast itself.
